SR&ED, explained plainly

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development program is a federal tax incentive administered by the Canada Revenue Agency — and it's the work we do most. It isn't a competitive grant you apply for in advance: you do the R&D during your fiscal year, then claim the credit with your corporate tax return. If the work qualifies, the credit is yours by right — which is why the quality of the claim matters so much.

Up to 35%
Refundable federal credit — CCPCs

Canadian-controlled private corporations can earn the enhanced 35% rate on up to $3 million of qualifying expenditures per year. "Refundable" means you receive it as a payment even if you owe no tax — vital for pre-profit innovators.

The $3M limit phases down as a corporation's taxable capital grows. We calculate your exact limit in the free assessment.

15%

Federal credit — other businesses

Corporations that aren't CCPCs, and CCPC spending above the enhanced limit, earn the general 15% federal investment tax credit, generally non-refundable and carried against taxes payable.

Still well worth claiming: unused credits can be carried back 3 years or forward 20 years.

8% + 3.5%

Ontario credits stack on top

Ontario adds its own incentives on the same R&D spending: the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (8%, refundable, for eligible corporations) and the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (3.5%, non-refundable).

Combined federal + Ontario support can return a substantial share of every R&D dollar — we model the combined figure for your business.

Does your work qualify? The CRA's three tests

Work qualifies as experimental development when it passes all three tests. This is the heart of every claim we write:

  • Technological uncertainty — the outcome couldn't be known in advance using standard, publicly available knowledge or routine practice.
  • Systematic investigation — you formed a hypothesis and tested it: prototypes, trials, iterations, measurements — not trial-and-error guesswork.
  • Technological advancement — the work generated new knowledge, whether the project succeeded or failed. A failed experiment can still be a valid claim.

Common qualifying work: new product development, process improvement, custom software and automation, prototyping, and solving technical problems that had no off-the-shelf answer.

What you can claim

Eligible work includes experimental development, applied research, basic research, and the support work directly tied to it. Claimable costs include:

  • Salaries & wages of staff doing the R&D
  • Materials consumed or transformed
  • Payments to Canadian contractors (generally 80% counts)
  • Overhead — via the CRA proxy method (55% of the salary base)
  • Certain equipment and shared-use costs
  • Work by universities & research institutes on your behalf

The most-missed item: owner and senior-staff time spent on technical problem-solving. If you worked on it, it likely belongs in the claim.

What usually does not qualify

The CRA excludes routine and commercial activity. Claiming these is the fastest route to a reduced or denied claim — we separate them out before filing:

  • Routine engineering, testing & quality control
  • Market research & sales promotion
  • Routine data collection
  • Commercial production & style changes
  • Using existing technology in a standard way
  • Social science & humanities research

Real projects usually mix qualifying and non-qualifying work. Splitting them correctly — and evidencing the qualifying part — is exactly where an experienced preparer earns their fee.

The one deadline you cannot miss: an SR&ED claim must be filed within 18 months of your tax year-end — for a December 31 year-end, that's June 30 of the second following year. After that date, the credit for that year is gone permanently, no exceptions. If last year's R&D hasn't been claimed yet, talk to us before anything else.

Paid your team last year? Part of those salaries can come back to you.

This is the point most business owners miss, so we'll say it plainly: SR&ED is retroactive. You don't need to apply before doing the work, and you don't need to have known the program existed. If last year you paid salaries to your personnel — engineers, developers, technicians, production staff, even your own salary as an owner working on the problem — and part of their time went into research and development work, the government can return a share of that money to you.

  • The research work counts, not the job title. If your people spent time developing a product, improving a process, building or fixing software, prototyping, testing, or solving technical problems with no ready-made answer — that time is R&D, even if nobody's title says "researcher."
  • Salaries are the biggest claimable cost. Wages are usually the largest part of an SR&ED claim — and the CRA's proxy method adds 55% on top of the salary base for overhead, so you claim more than the wages alone.
  • It can be cash back, not just a tax break. For eligible CCPCs the credit is refundable — if your company owes little or no tax, the CRA pays the credit out. The work is already done and the salaries are already paid; the claim is how you recover part of them.
  • Even failed projects count. If the research didn't succeed commercially, the eligible work can still qualify — what matters is that your team genuinely investigated a technical problem.

A simplified example: your team spent $200,000 of last year's salaries on qualifying development work. Add the 55% proxy amount for overhead and the claim base becomes $310,000. At the 35% enhanced federal rate, that's roughly $108,500 back — before Ontario credits — from salaries you already paid. Your real figure depends on your limit and how much of the work qualifies, which is exactly what our free assessment calculates.

What we do: we go through last year's payroll and projects with you, identify the research work hidden inside regular jobs, document it the way the CRA requires, and file the claim before the 18-month deadline closes.

Well-known programs we help you apply to

SR&ED and IRAP lead the list — they're our specialty. Around them sits the wider set of programs Canadian businesses ask us about. Eligibility rules and amounts change with each intake — we verify the current rules for your business before applying.

SR&ED Tax Credits

Federal · CRA — Specialty
Up to 35% enhanced credit for eligible CCPCs

Canada's largest R&D incentive, and the core of our practice. Refundable and non-refundable tax credits on eligible experimental development work — including work many businesses don't realize qualifies, and work already completed last fiscal year.

Best for: businesses doing technical problem-solving, product development or process improvement. Full SR&ED guide ↓

NRC IRAP

Federal — Specialty
Project funding + advisory services

Canada's flagship innovation program, and the natural partner to SR&ED: IRAP funds R&D projects as you undertake them, while SR&ED credits the eligible costs afterward. Advisory support from an Industrial Technology Advisor, plus financial contributions for technology innovation projects at SMEs.

Best for: incorporated businesses developing or improving technology, products or processes.

CanExport SMEs

Federal
Up to $50,000 · up to 50% of eligible costs

Cost-sharing for export development: international trade shows, market research, IP protection abroad, and adapting marketing tools for foreign markets.

Best for: SMEs entering or expanding into markets outside Canada.

Canada Summer Jobs & Wage Subsidies

Federal
Wage subsidies per eligible hire

Federal and provincial wage-subsidy programs that reimburse part of the wages for youth, students, newcomers and other targeted hires, plus apprenticeship incentives in the trades.

Best for: businesses planning to hire in the next 12 months.

FedDev Ontario & Regional Funds

Ontario · Regional
Cost-shared contributions

Southern Ontario's regional development agency funds business scale-up, productivity and community economic development projects, alongside Ontario provincial programs.

Best for: Ontario businesses investing in growth, equipment or new capacity.

Municipal & Local Incentives

Municipal
Rebates & fee relief varies by city

City-level programs — including Toronto incentives for façade improvements, energy retrofits, main-street businesses and development charge relief — that owners routinely overlook.

Best for: businesses with a physical location investing in their premises.

Why businesses miss this money

It's rarely about eligibility. It's about time, timing and paperwork.

  • Programs are scattered. Federal departments, provincial ministries, regional agencies and cities each run their own — there is no single list, and names change constantly.
  • Windows are short. Many intakes open for only a few weeks a year. Missing the date usually means waiting a full year.
  • Weak applications get cut. Reviewers score against published criteria. A complete, well-evidenced application is the difference between a cheque and a rejection letter.
  • Approval isn't the finish line. Claims, receipts and progress reports decide whether approved money actually gets paid. We stay through that part too.

Built for owners, not bureaucrats

KA.78896 is a Toronto-based consultancy for small and mid-sized businesses — shops, restaurants, manufacturers, trades, tech startups and service firms. If you have a business number and a plan, you're exactly who these programs were designed for.

  • Plain language, always. We translate program rules into a short list of what to do, what it pays, and by when.
  • English & Persian service. Immigrant and newcomer business owners can work through the whole process in Farsi if they prefer.
  • Honest odds. If a program is a poor fit, we'll tell you before you spend a dollar — and point you to the one that fits better.

Questions owners ask us

Does my business actually qualify for government grants?+
Most incorporated Canadian businesses — and many sole proprietors — qualify for something. Programs typically look at your industry, size, location, how long you've been operating, and what the money is for. The free eligibility check on this page gives a first indication; the free consultation confirms it program by program.
Do I have to pay a grant back?+
True grants and wage subsidies do not need to be repaid, as long as you spend the money as approved and complete the reporting. Some programs are instead repayable contributions or low-interest loans — we always tell you which type a program is before you apply, so there are no surprises.
How long does an application take?+
Preparing a strong application usually takes one to three weeks once we have your documents. Government review times vary widely by program — from a few weeks to several months. That's exactly why starting before an intake deadline matters, and why we track the calendar for you.
Can you guarantee my application will be approved?+
No honest consultant can — approval decisions are made by government reviewers, and many programs are competitive. What we guarantee is a complete, on-time, well-evidenced application that matches the program's scoring criteria, and straight advice when a program is a long shot.
We paid our staff salaries last year and they did development work. Can we still get money back?+
Very likely, yes — this is exactly how SR&ED works. The program is claimed after the fact, on work already done. If part of your personnel's paid time last year went into research or development — building, prototyping, testing, or solving technical problems — a share of those salaries (plus a 55% proxy amount for overhead) can come back as a tax credit, refundable for eligible CCPCs. You don't need to have applied in advance or even known the program existed. The one condition is timing: the claim must be filed within 18 months of your tax year-end. Bring us last year's payroll and project list and we'll identify what qualifies — free.
Our R&D project failed. Is the work still claimable?+
Often, yes. SR&ED rewards the investigation, not commercial success. If your team faced a genuine technological uncertainty and tested approaches systematically, the work can qualify even if the product never launched. What matters is evidence: notes, prototypes, test results and records of what was tried. We help you reconstruct and present that evidence properly.
My business is brand new. Is there anything for me?+
Yes, though the mix is different: startup-oriented programs, digital adoption support, youth and newcomer entrepreneur programs, and local incentives tend to be the best fit early on. Revenue-generating programs like SR&ED and IRAP open up as you grow — we map both in your assessment.
Can we work together in Persian?+
Yes. Consultations, explanations and progress updates can all be done in Persian (Farsi) — تمام مراحل مشاوره و پیگیری به زبان فارسی هم انجام می‌شود — while applications themselves are prepared in English (or French where a program requires it), as governments require.
What do you need from me to start?+
Just the basics for the free assessment: what your business does, where it's located, how many people you employ, and what you're planning (hiring, equipment, a new product, exporting…). Financial statements and incorporation documents come later, only for the programs we actually file.
